column3: Its use of yamhaq shows divine obliteration, sharpening the claim that Allah effaces riba.
It immediately frames acceptable spending as giving from good earnings and produce.
Allah's refusal to love the arrogant broadens the moral force of His disapproval, without addressing riba.
Allah's rejection of the treacherous unbeliever reinforces the verse's disapproval of culpable disbelief and sin.
Wisdom and abundant good in the same passage support discerning true benefit beyond apparent increase.
Love here concerns victory and does not clarify riba or sadaqah.
It checks pride and attachment to what one receives, qualifying how material increase is valued.
It immediately affirms that Allah knows every expenditure and vowed offering.
Divine love is tied to following, but it adds no financial or destructive-growth detail.
Its exact pairing of treachery and sin closely illuminates the rejected kafar athim.
It immediately contrasts fear of poverty with Allah's promise of forgiveness and bounty.
It explicitly presents sadaqah as aid to the distressed and links it to divine recompense.
Allah is said to receive the charities, giving sadaqah direct divine orientation.
It immediately promises reward and freedom from fear and grief for continual spending.
It explicitly says charitable giving is multiplied, clarifying yurbi as divine increase.
The fate of every stubborn kafar reinforces the gravity of the verse's kafar designation.
It directly commands believers to leave the remainder of riba.
It names taking riba as forbidden and as consuming people's wealth falsely.
The repeated description affak athim reinforces the moral weight of athim.
It immediately treats charity as good, especially when given to the poor, and as expiating wrongs.
Its rabiyah punishment suggests excess in a different context, with little bearing on riba.
It repeats the affak athim characterization, reinforcing the verse's condemnation of sinfulness.
It directly distinguishes permitted trade from forbidden riba and describes riba's consequence.
The earth's reviving and rising after rain supplies a natural image of life-giving increase.
It protects voluntary charitable giving, including small contributions, from contempt.
It immediately requires respite for debtors in hardship and calls remission better.
The sprouting of grain supplies only a minimal image of increase.
It specifies the ordained recipients of sadaqat, giving the positive side concrete social direction.
It immediately says spending is for one's own good and will be repaid without injustice.
Preferring disbelief to faith is a moral contrast, not an explanation of riba or sadaqah.
The description of the sinful transgressor reinforces athim as a serious moral charge.
It immediately states the rewarded, fearless state of believers who give zakah.
Familial preference expressed by ahabb does not illuminate the financial contrast.
Allah rewards and loves those who do good, supporting the positive moral horizon of sadaqah.
Personal earning and liability before Allah support the passage's accounting of financial conduct.
Love of the immediate world over a weighty future cautions against judging gain by immediacy.
Withholding good while being sinful provides a negative moral counterpart to charitable increase.
It identifies restrained poor people as recipients and affirms Allah's knowledge of every good spent.
Allah's dislike of excess gives a broader limit on material behavior, though not riba specifically.
It exposes self-interested resentment over charity distribution, clarifying a corrupt response to sadaqat.
It gives detailed rules for just, documented debt, distinguishing fair obligation from riba.
The pledge to give sadaqah from Allah's bounty supports charity as a response to provision.
It directly forbids consuming riba as multiplied multiples.
It immediately demands repentance, limits claims to principal, and forbids mutual wrong.
Reward from divine bounty for believers and righteous action supports the verse's moral accounting.
Allah's unrestricted giving contrasts with constricted possession, while corruption is explicitly unloved.
It continues the debt ethic with trust, repayment, and the sin of concealing testimony.
Love of the immediate is a relevant warning against preferring apparent present gain.
Persistent disbelief and its curse reinforce the severity of the kafar description.
It closes the riba sequence with return to Allah and full, just repayment for what each earned.
Allah's dislike of aggression supports justice generally but not the financial contrast.
Humanity is called zalum kaffar despite abundant gifts, closely echoing the verse's final wording.
Allah's ownership and accounting of hidden and open matters complete the surrounding moral accountability.
Love directed to rivals instead of Allah concerns devotion rather than riba or charity.
Unrepentant disbelief and withheld forgiveness reinforce the warning bound to kafar.
Belief, hearing, obedience, and return to Allah frame the response required by the nearby commands.
It calls charity, kindness, and reconciliation good when sought for Allah's pleasure, with great reward.
The liar and kafar are denied guidance, reinforcing the verse's censure of disbelief.
It immediately subordinates harmful charity to kind speech and forgiveness, defining sound giving.
Establishing truth and nullifying falsehood supplies a general pattern for the contrast between riba and sadaqah.
Affirming the husna does not itself explain the financial contrast.
The rule on public evil speech has only a distant connection to divine disapproval.
What is loved may be harmful, challenging the appearance that monetary increase is true good.
It directs wealth to kin, the needy, and travelers while forbidding waste.
Allah loves equitable dealing, supporting the just social order opposed to exploitative gain.
It contrasts punishment for hypocrisy and idolatry with repentance for believers, reinforcing moral consequence.
It directly commands spending and links it with ihsan, which Allah loves.
Allah's unique dominion is foundational but adds no specific financial meaning.
Preferring worldly life over the hereafter connects misplaced preference with disbelief.
Allah fully pays believers for righteous deeds and does not love wrongdoers.
Divine love of repentance and purity does not clarify riba or sadaqah.
Allah's dislike of the boastful cautions against the pride that can accompany wealth.
Loving advisers in this narrative does not add to the verse's financial or moral contrast.
It defines corruption as destroying tillage and offspring, making harmful outcomes a clear counterpoint to true growth.
A false claim to divine love and ensuing judgment adds little to riba or sadaqah.
Turning from obedience is linked to those Allah does not love, reinforcing the demand to heed prohibition.
It shows that charity can be nullified by reproach, injury, and display, distinguishing real from void giving.
Allah's dislike of wrongdoers places changing worldly conditions within a moral judgment.
It depicts people Allah loves through humility, resolve, and striving, supplying a positive contrast to rejected traits.
It commands beneficence to dependents and vulnerable neighbors while condemning proud boasting.
It makes giving wealth to vulnerable people a defining component of birr.
Love of purification has no direct bearing on riba or charitable increase.
Preferring worldly life and seeking a crooked path gives a relevant warning about distorted valuation.
It gives the seed-and-harvest image and explicit multiplication for spending in Allah's path.
The bestowed love in the Moses narrative does not illuminate the financial contrast.
Allah's love for the steadfast supports a moral orientation toward enduring faithful action.
Intense love of khayr may caution attachment to possessions, but the reference is not specific.
Reciprocal interpersonal love in a hostile setting does not clarify the verse.
Loving khayr to the point of neglecting remembrance warns against wealth-like attachment displacing devotion.
Faith is made beloved while disbelief, defiance, and disobedience are made hateful, sharpening the moral polarity.
The mention of Allah's kindled fire alone adds no specific explanatory link.
Allah as sole creator and possessor of benefit and harm gives only a general theological basis.
It exposes verbal belief without heart-faith, lying, and distortion, relevant to the verse's disbelief-and-sin censure.
The general command to fear Allah and obey adds no particular detail about riba or sadaqah.
Gratitude and righteous action after parental care offer only a distant ethical support.
Allah's watchfulness gives a general accountability frame without specific financial content.
Broken promises and lying produce hypocrisy, reinforcing the seriousness of sinful unfaithfulness.
The messenger reciting purified pages does not clarify the verse's contrast.
The nearness and unknown timing of the Hour provides only a broad accountability horizon.
Choosing blindness over guidance and receiving punishment broadly supports consequences of culpable choice.
It directly denies that riba given to increase among people grows with Allah, while zakah seeking His face is multiplied.
It directs what is spent toward parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers.
It answers what should be spent with al-afw, making charitable outflow a direct subject.
It calls spending a good loan to Allah and explicitly promises multiplied return.
It commands spending before the day when trade, friendship, and intercession fail.
It preserves the reward of spending by forbidding reminders of generosity and injury.
Its garden image depicts sincere spending as a yield that grows securely.
Its ruined garden image warns how a person's productive wealth can be lost when need is greatest.
It makes spending from what one loves a condition of attaining birr.
It praises those who spend in ease and hardship as doers of good whom Allah loves.
It rebukes withholding from what Allah provided and connects spending in Allah's way to faith.
It presents freeing and, where unavailable, fasting or charity within redress for wrongful killing.
It joins zakah and a good loan to Allah with forgiveness and reward.
It calls relinquishing a due claim as charity an expiation.
It commands giving the harvest's due on harvest day and forbids excess.
It condemns hoarding gold and silver rather than spending it in Allah's way.
It portrays hoarded wealth as a source of punishment, exposing false security in accumulation.
It links rejected contributions to disbelief, disobedience, and reluctant giving.
It distinguishes a view of spending as loss from its faithful alternative.
It presents spending as nearness to Allah and a means of receiving mercy.
It commands taking charity that purifies and grows the giver.
It describes those who spend secretly and openly and repel evil with good.
It commands believing servants to establish prayer and spend secretly and openly before the final day.
It forbids both clenched withholding and ruinous overextension in spending.
Zakah is joined to prayer and lasting blessedness.
Commanding prayer and zakah marks the prophet's care for righteous practice.
Prayer, zakah, and doing good are given as guided obligations.
The steadfast are described as those who establish prayer and spend from what they receive.
Zakah accompanies establishing prayer, commanding right, and forbidding wrong.
The believers are characterized by active concern for zakah.
Neither trade nor sale distracts the faithful from prayer, zakah, and the Day of accounting.
It orders seeking the hereafter through Allah's gift, doing good, and avoiding corruption.
It gives kin, the needy, and travelers their due as the better course for those seeking Allah's face.
The faithful spend from what they are provided alongside hope and fear of Allah.
Zakah is commanded alongside prayer and obedience in the household's moral formation.
Charitable men and women are promised forgiveness and great reward.
Whatever is spent is replaced by Allah, explicitly opposing fear that giving merely diminishes wealth.
Reciting, establishing prayer, and spending secretly and openly are called a commerce that will not fail.
Consultation, prayer, and spending from provision define the faithful community.
Those called to spend are warned that stinginess harms themselves and that Allah can replace them.
The wealthy are said to have an acknowledged right for the petitioner and deprived person.
It commands spending from what humans hold as successors and promises a great reward to believers who do so.
It distinguishes earlier and later spending, affirming both receive the good promise.
It again calls spending a good loan to Allah and promises multiplication and generous reward.
Stinginess and urging others to stinginess are condemned against Allah's self-sufficiency.
It requires a charity before private consultation, joining sincere approach with financial giving.
When the prior charity requirement is not met, prayer, zakah, and obedience remain explicitly enjoined.
It orders public wealth not to circulate only among the rich, a direct social counterpoint to extractive increase.
It commands spending before death, when regret over missed charity is too late.
It calls spending for one's own good and warns against the soul's stinginess.
It scales support to means and provision, grounding spending in capacity rather than exploitation.
It describes a known right in wealth for the petitioner and deprived person.
It joins prayer, zakah, and a good loan to Allah with an assurance of greater good and reward.
It praises feeding the needy, orphan, and captive despite love for the food.
Feeding in a day of severe hunger gives concrete form to liberating charitable action.
Giving while fearing Allah begins a sequence whose path is eased toward the good.
It describes the one who gives wealth to purify himself.
Sincere worship, prayer, and zakah are presented together as upright religion.
Rivalry in accumulation gives a direct warning against treating increase itself as the goal.
Gathering and counting wealth supplies a negative image of numerical accumulation.
Failure to urge feeding the poor identifies a social negation of the charitable side of the verse.
